metadata.title: Precise ablation of cholesteatoma using a 445-nm diode laser

sections.text: In cholesteatoma surgery, precise tissue resection is important, as the diseased tissue needs to be completely removed while preserving the ossicular chain to prevent recurrence and hearing loss. The ability to precisely ablate tissue using a pulsed diode laser operating in single-trigger mode was investigated. Single laser pulses with a duration of were applied with a power ranging from via a multimode optical fiber. Fiber distance to tissue was varied from , and irradiation angles from . Porcine ear cartilage with remaining perichondrium on top served to represent the human ossicle structure with cholesteatoma. Further ablation experiments were performed on human cholesteatoma and ossicle samples. Ablation craters were measured by optical coherence tomography (OCT), and tissue damage assessed with haematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections. The ablation depth reached up to when operating at power output without causing damage to the underlying cartilage. Laser pulses with successfully ablated cholesteatoma, but did not damage the ossicles. The results show that a diode laser pulses can be used to effectively remove cholesteatoma, potentially preserving ossicles and hearing ability.

Chronic middle ear infection (otitis media) is one of the most common ear diseases worldwide and is estimated to affect more than 20 million people 1 . Approximately one quarter of the patients develop cholesteatoma over time – a special form of otitis media characterized by the ingrowth of keratinizing squamous epithelium into the middle ear 2 – 4 . Cholesteatomas often remain undetected for years, and initial symptoms such as tinnitus, purulent otorrhea, or increasing hearing loss usually only appear once the ossicular chain has already been damaged 5 , 6 . Patients with cholesteatoma have to be treated with surgery 7 . Although the standard procedure for mastoidectomy has been shown to be effective, it can be associated with complications such as hearing loss, delayed wound healing, facial nerve paralysis, vertigo, loss of taste, and an increased risk of infection 1 , 8 , 9 . Depending on the clinical situation, mastoidectomy can be performed with or without creation of a radical cavity. To illustrate the clinical situation, Fig. 1 shows examples of the delicate morphology of the stapes and cholesteatoma tissue. The invasive growth of cholesteatoma and the associated destruction of bone structures in the middle ear is associated with inflammation and immunological processes and represent a considerable challenge in otology 4 , 10 , 11 . Given the delicate anatomy of the middle ear, particular attention must be paid to the small dimensions of the structures that need to be preserved. The stapes typically measures in height and in width at the footplate, whereas the fine structures of the posterior and anterior crus measure between and 12 – 17 . The width of the incus is 12 , 13 , 18 , 19 . The head of the malleus has a width of approx. and at the neck it has a width of 12 , 13 , 20 . This range ( ) reflects both the fine structural thicknesses and the overall size of individual components within the middle ear. Surgeons need to perform their procedures with precise accuracy because the ossicular chain has fragile structures. The effective removal of diseased tissue using laser-based techniques shows good potential, as these methods enable controlled tissue removal with minimal damage to the surrounding healthy tissue and the delicate middle ear ossicles. Preservation of the ossicular chain has been shown to be associated with improved postoperative hearing outcomes, and laser-assisted techniques may facilitate this by enabling precise tissue removal 21 – 23 . As a result, minimally invasive procedures are becoming increasingly important. In general, laser technology offers promising possibilities in this context, as it enables the efficient and gentle removal of diseased tissue 22 , 24 , 25 . Lasers used in ENT surgery range in wavelength from the infrared (CO 2 -laser: ; Er:YAG laser: ) to the visible region (Argon: , Nd:YAG laser frequency doupled with a KTP crystal: ) 22 , 26 . With an absorption coefficient of water of , the CO 2 laser radiation rapidly vaporizes tissue and coagulates small blood vessels simultaneously in a very thin zone. However, for guiding light for endoscopic surgeries, hollow-core fibers have to be used that are less flexible and more expensive than standard fibers 26 . Also, for hemostasis in vascular tissue, a slightly greater penetration depth and high absorption specificially in hemoglobin is beneficial. In cholesteatoma surgery, the KTP laser with an absorption coefficient of in water and in blood ( HbO 2 /Hb per litre) is preferred so far 26 – 28 . Since some years, diode lasers with a wavelength of are available with a higher absorption coefficient in hemoglobin and therefore an excellent ability of coagulation with a limited depth of penetration during surgical inciscions ( ) 24 , 28 , 29 . Compared to other photoangiolytic lasers like the KTP laser (and pulsed dye lasers), the blue laser is, in addition to the increased absorption in hemoglobin, utilizing an enormous technical simplification by pumping the laser with a semiconductor (diode), thus avoiding complex technical constructions and maintenance services 30 . Combined with its ability in noncontact cutting and availability in flexible fibers, it is ideal for endoscopic, single-handed surgeries, allowing the laser to reach and obliterate disease at angled anatomical sites 31 . The diode laser was shown to be versatile and effective in other subspecialties of otorhinolaryngology 32 , 33 and Tam et al. showed in their retrospective cohort study that its use is safe in cholesteatoma surgery 31 : After partial microsurgical removal, the 445 nm diode laser can be used in clinical practice to specifically eliminate any remaining cholesteatoma tissue. The aim of this work is to investigate the use of a diode laser in single-pulse mode for the ablation of cholesteatoma tissue while preserving the ossicular structures. Pig ear cartilage was used as a tissue model to investigate ablation with single pulses of a diode laser, porcine tissue represents a well-established experimental model with comparable optical properties 34 – 36 . For example, the absorption coefficient of human cholesteatoma at (average value ) lies near the range reported for soft tissues such as subcutaneous adipose tissue ( ), and similar values have been reported for the reduced scattering coefficient (cholesteatoma: , subcutaneous adipose tissue: µ' s ~1.4mm -1 ) 37 , 54 . To simulate clinically realistic conditions, the samples were covered with a thin layer of blood, and single pulses, partly in overlapping sequences, were applied to replicate surgical resection paths. The pulse duration and power range were selected based on previous pulsed-laser studies and the concept of thermal relaxation time, aiming to limit heat diffusion and confine the effect to superficial tissue layers 24 , 38 , 39 . The main objective is to determine parameter values which support both safe operation and reliable application results. The analysis of the influence of laser power, fiber distance, angle of incidence, and pulse overlap should show how these parameters determine the ablation behavior of the tissue. In addition, samples of human cholesteatoma and middle ear ossicles were used to test the transferability of the results to clinical conditions. In the long term, the findings may contribute to improving the precision of laser-assisted procedures, potentially reducing the risk of thermal or mechanical damage to the ossicles, and thus may supporting the preservation of hearing.

sections.section: Ablation Of Superficial Tissue Layers On Cartilage Model Using Single Pulses
sections.text: The ablation depth showed a increase in both groups in the power range of for single -pulses (Fig. 2 a). Each data point represents one measurement on a tissue samples, with the number of measurements varying due to differences in sample availability. This experiment involved analyzing both porcine cartilage and human cholesteatoma tissue to verify the comparability of the ablation depths. Ablation depths of were achieved in human tissue and in porcine tissue when operating at power levels between . At an average power of , the values in the porcine model were , with no macroscopic damage to the underlying cartilage. At , maximum ablation depths of (human) and (porcine) were achieved. Differences between human and porcine tissue were minor overall, confirming the porcine model as suitable. Linear fits (based on the steady state thermal ablation model, see discussion) result in a R 2 value of 0.75 for human cholesteatoma and 0.7 for porcine cartilage with residual tissue, supporting the use of a linear approximation within the investigated parameter range. The relatively large standard deviations can be attributed to the inherent variability of biological tissue, including differences in tissue thickness, composition, and blood content, as well as small variations in manual fiber positioning during the experiments. The histological analyzis supported the OCT measurement data. H&E staining revealed precise ablation of the superficial tissue layer (perichondrium), while the cartilage matrix remained intact throughout (Fig. 2 b). Across all tested power settings, the underlying cartilage showed no structural alterations. The outer tissue layers were successfully removed without damaging the cartilage structure beneath.

sections.section: Influence Of Varying Fiber Position On The Ablation Depth
sections.text: In several fiber guide variations, the effects of fiber spacing and the angle of incidence (angle between the fiber and the tissue surface) on the ablation depth in cartilage with a residual layer were systematically investigated. The results demonstrated that both parameters affected the ablation depth, and the data confirm that precise tissue removal is achievable even with manual fiber guidance (Fig. 3 ). The ablation depth decreases with increased distance between the fiber and the tissue surface. The average ablation depth reached at distance but it decreased to at and then reached at ( , puls duration, Fig. 4 a). OCT images confirm that the ablation remains limited to the superficial residual layer, while the underlying cartilage remains structurally intact. The fit curves shown in Fig. 3 a were adjusted using the equation , with being the fiber radius and the spot radius on the tissue for distance (coefficient of determination for ). With this equation the ablation depths follows the quadratic decrease in fluence corresponding to the increase in area (assumption: steady-state model of thermal ablation, see discussion). The angle of incidence influences both the shape and depth of the ablation crater. Flat angles produced wide, flat, and elliptical ablation zones, while a vertical incidence ( ) enabled the deepest ablation. The average ablation depth increased continuously with increasing angle (Fig. 4 b). At , depths of were achieved, while at , depths of were already achieved. In the maximum configuration ( ), the values were up to . This increase can be attributed to the smaller irradiated area and the resulting higher energy density at a steeper angle of incidence. The OCT images in Fig. 4 illustrate this angle-dependent increase in ablation depth. This increase can be attributed to the smaller irradiated area and the resulting higher energy density at a steeper angle of incidence: The spot size on the tissue is proportional to (Fig. 8 for explanatory drawing). Accordingly, the fit curves shown in Fig. 3 b were adjusted using the equation ( for ). Under manual fiber guidance, small variations in fiber distance of up to and angle variation of can be assumed based on the experimental setup and handling conditions, resulting in differences in ablation depth of approximately for each parameter varying separately or up to combining distance and angle variations (assumption: quadratic error propagation).

Overlapping single pulses with a power of and a pulse duration of were applied to cartilage tissue with a residual layer to simulate clinical common situation where tissue removal requires repeated laser application rather than a single pulse. The spot diameter was approximately , as calculated from the fiber geometry and divergence angle (Fig. 8 ) and the distances between the spots were and . This overlap created a continuous ablation area. The OCT analyses showed uniform ablation patterns with depths ranging from to , depending on the remaining tissue thickness (Fig. 5 ). Particularly with a thinner residual tissue layer on top, uniform and controlled ablation was achieved. The OCT data were used for quantitative evaluation of the ablation depth, while the cross-sectional images in Fig. 5 illustrate the ablation morphology. Across all examined samples, no structural damage to the underlying cartilage was observed. Given that the thickness of the residual tissue layer ranged between approximately 420 and 560 µm, the measured ablation depths were always restricted to the soft tissue layer above the cartilage.

sections.section: Laser Ablation Of Human Ossicles And Cholesteatoma Tissue
sections.text: In order to validate the results from porcine tissue models, comparative studies were performed on human samples ( , pulse duration, , results depicted in Fig. 2 a). Both cholesteatoma tissue and malleus and incus bones were used. Porcine blood was additionally applied to the cholesteatoma sample, but not to the ossicle samples. The OCT images showed clearly visible morphological differences between the tissues. As the laser power increased, the crater size in the porcine tissue increased continuously and was predominantly round to angular in shape, with superficial bulges indicating the remaining residual tissue. In contrast, the human ossicles showed only pointed craters or no ablative changes at all (Fig. 6 a). At a power of , no ablation could be detected in the cartilage tissue of the human ossicles. At a power of , signs of damage to the ossicles were visible ( ). At a power of , the ablation depths were clearly smaller ( ). In contrast, cholesteatoma tissue showed clear and reproducible ablation effects at and a depth of up to . Overall, the human ossicles exhibited significantly reduced ablation behavior (Fig. 6 b). At , the ablation depth was only about of the values measured in porcine cartilage samples and in cholesteatoma. Since there was no residual soft tissue or only small blood vessels present on the human ossicles, this lower ablation depth results from the lower absorption of mineralized bone compared to soft tissue or blood-covered tissue. This reflects the clinical situation, in which cholesteatoma matrix is often present on the periosteum of the ossicles, which must be carefully removed to prevent recurrence while preserving hearing.

As already mentioned in the introduction, ENT surgeons can choose from a range of lasers with different wavelengths and pulse characteristics. The diode laser, due to the high absorption in hemoglobin and melanin, is expected to have good photoangiolytic properties and reduce intraoperative bleeding and scarring 40 . While differentiation from CO 2 lasers is relatively clear due to the significant difference in absorption in water and hemoglobin, the question arises as to how the wavelength compares to “green” lasers such as the KTP laser with . Several studies report that the laser has similar, but superior properties to KTP laser, including a better hemostatic effect, minimal water absorption hence minimizing injuries to the inner ear, and higher tissue absorption rate, which allows operating at lower power hence less thermal injuries 31 . Actually, there are studies showing an advantage of the laser compared to the KTP laser in laryngology 40 . Lin et al. e.g. found that the ‘blue laser’ resulted in less vocal fold scarring compared to the KTP laser in normal rat vocal folds 41 . Balouch et al. conducted a study on 31 subjects diagnosed with vascular lesions of the vocal folds, in which the blue laser was used in pulsed mode at low power densities ( ). They found that it was less effective in preventing recurrence of vascular lesions on the vocal folds compared to the KTP laser, However, postoperative edema and haemorrhage were less severe in patients treated with the blue laser, indicating reduced thermal trauma 40 , 42 . In contrast, Hanke et al. performed an experimental study with gingiva tissue with diode lasers ranging from to and found a higher cutting efficiency for compared to the near-infrared range ( ), but not to 24 . For cholesteatoma surgery, another aspect of 445 nm radiation might be beneficial: blue light has been utilized in other areas of medicine for bacterial decontamination 43 , 44 . However, Tam et al. found no reduction in residual rate in a study including 120 cholesteatoma cases ( surgeries using the laser) 31 . Further studies are ongoing. Based on these considerations, this research demonstrates the high potential of the diode laser for precise ablation in the middle ear region. With single laser pulses, small tissue volumes with a thickness can be removed. Cholesteatoma tissue with a thin blood layer was effectively ablated even at low power levels, whereas the compact structures of the ossicles showed a higher ablation threshold (Fig. 6 ). These differences in ablation behavior confirm the possibility of targeted removal of pathological areas while preserving functionally relevant structures. The ablation depth can be controlled by various parameters, such as power, fiber spacing, and beam angle. This has also been confirmed in other studies. Braun et al. demonstrated that a wavelength of in soft tissue enables high cutting performance with minimal thermal damage to the surrounding areas 39 . With a steady-state ablation model (see e.g. 38 ), neglecting heat diffusion or plume shielding, the ablation depth is given by with being the effective absorption coefficient, the fluence and the threshold fluence. Using a Taylor approximation of the logarithm, the depth thus follows a linear relationship with power when this model is valid. Hanke et al. showed a nearly linear relationship between power and incision depth for different diode wavelengths ( , continuous wave (cw) operation), which corresponds to our single-pulse measurements 24 . The depth values we measured with single pulses are also consistent with a linear dependence – the value for the fit on the human cholesteatoma samples is and for porcine tissue. The high intersection point of the adjustment curve for the pig data with the y-axis is noteworthy, as an intersection point is expected for a threshold process such as thermal ablation. This will be investigated further. However, it should be noted that there is considerable variation in the values. In human cholesteatoma samples, this is already due to the considerable variation in tissue type and blood content in the samples. The homogeneity is significantly higher in animal tissue samples. Here, inaccuracies in fiber positioning, possible contamination of the fiber during pulse emission, and varying onset of ablation of weakly absorbing tissue (low blood content) contribute to the variance. Nevertheless, at a distance of and medium power levels, the values all stay within a range of a few hundred micrometers, without macroscopic damage to the cartilage. Even at maximum power, the depths remained below the critical dimensions of delicate ear structures at around (Fig. 2 a). This clearly indicates that a single pulse would not cut through the ossicles. These dimensions are surgically relevant, as the anatomical vulnerability points of the ossicles are of a similar order of size. The total height of the stapes is typically , with the crus thickness at its narrowest point being 12 – 17 . The widths of the malleus and incus are in the millimeter range 12 , 13 , 18 – 20 . Ablation depths below are therefore surgically advantageous, as they allow very precise tissue removal with less than ablation depth per pulse and ensure that a single pulse does not completely transect the ossicles. In all cases, histological examination of the underlying cartilage revealed no structural damage. The procedure thus demonstrated its effectiveness as a method for removing cholesteatoma tissue while preserving the ossicular chain, which could be confirmed in a clinical study using the wavelength laser 45 . The distance between the fiber and the tissue has a strong influence on ablation. As the distance increases, the spot diameter increases, the energy density decreases, and the ablation depth decreases 30 . The ablation width in porcine cartilage with remaining tissue reached at distance but expanded to at distance when using power. At low power ( ), the ablation width even decreased with increasing distance. The results confirm a quadratic correlation between ablation depth and distance 30 . In clinical practice, distances of are common, so the aim is to achieve precise ablation with single pulses. Under these realistic conditions during manual fiber guidance, small deviations in distance and angle are inevitable and lead to slight variations in the measured ablation depth, typically in the range of . The small differences in ablation depth occur because of minimal variations in local energy delivery but remain within an acceptable range. The laser power requires precise optimization based on tissue structure because both uneven surfaces and manual guidance methods impact the achieved results. Nevertheless, this indicates that controlled tissue removal can still be achieved even under manual handling. In addition, the complex geometry and curved surfaces of middle ear structures such as the ossicles make it difficult to maintain a constant irradiation angle, which may further influence the local fluence and thus the ablation depth. The angle of incidence also plays a decisive role. If the fiber is held at an angle to the surface, an elliptical laser spot is created. Flatter angles result in a larger irradiated area and thus lower energy density 46 . Our data show that at degree and , the deepest ablation was at the point of the elliptical crater closest to the fiber end, where the intensity of the Gaussian beam is highest 47 . It can be assumed that angles between and are used in clinical practice. Measurements of the ablation depth in porcine cartilage with residual tissue at ranged between and . Irregular surfaces and manual guidance can lead to variations, although these remained within the safe range. Letting the laser spots overlap , uniform resection paths could be created without enlarging the damage zones in the peripheral area. The OCT data showed that ablation depth stayed constant between to in all examined residual tissue thicknesses. In addition, the ablation depth can be controlled via the pulse energy. Thicker tissue layers can be removed step by step, which is an important aspect in avoiding complications. The laser therefore can be used for tissue resections without damaging ossicular structures. In this study, OCT was primarily used to quantify the ablation depth. However, OCT has increasingly been investigated as an imaging modality for middle ear structures. Several studies have shown that OCT can be used to visualize middle ear structures and may help to distinguish cholesteatoma from surrounding tissue 48 – 51 . These findings suggest that OCT may not only serve as a quantitative tool but also has potential for intraoperative assessment of middle ear pathology. The amount of control over the depth of ablation does not necessarily correlate with clinical “safe” versus “unsafe” threshold values. Available literature provides mainly qualitative recommendations rather than clearly defined limits. For example, Yau et al. state in their paper on endoscopic cholesteatoma surgery using a laser that, in their experience, the laser should not be focused directly on the bone for an extended period, as this can result in bone injury. They also note that lasering should be stopped immediately once charring of the bone is visible 52 . However, carbonization already indicates at least superficial damage to the bone. The authors also mention that a perilymphatic fistula may occur when the stapes footplate is lasered. They suggest first removing gross disease with instruments, followed by the application of a defocused laser to any residual tissue. The laser was most frequently used to ablate cholesteatoma from the stapes superstructure. Tam et al. note that, in cholesteatoma surgeries using the diode laser, they took care to avoid applying the laser to vulnerable structures, including the facial nerve, the oval and round windows, and the dehiscent semicircular canals 31 . In addition, there are many tissue characteristics that can vary from patient to patient, and can significantly affect the surgical treatment (e.g., thickness of the bony specimen, inflammation, vascularization). In CW mode, heat input accumulates due to continuous energy delivery, whereas in single-pulse mode, the energy is delivered for a short time and the tissue is able to cool down in between pulses. If the pulse duration is within the range of the thermal relaxation time, the effect is limited to the superficial layers 53 . Studies on gingiva showed significantly broader and deeper thermal influence zones in CW mode, which further supports the use of single-pulse mode for working close to bone 24 . Blood absorbs strongly in the range of . Wisotzky et al. showed that the absorption properties of cholesteatoma change significantly when blood is applied, since a characteristic hemoglobin peak occurs between and 37 . In our experiments, porcine blood was applied to all samples except the human ossicles. A thin blood layer on the tissue surface can enhance energy uptake at due to these hemoglobin peaks, supporting effective soft-tissue ablation 25 . In our experiments, porcine blood was applied to all samples except the human ossicles, allowing a direct comparison between blood-covered and non-covered tissue. The results demonstrate the ability to reliably estimate the ablation properties at this wavelength for both the tissue and the surrounding structures. Human cholesteatoma could already be removed at , a power at which the ossicles showed no alterations. This can be explained by structural differences, as mineralized bone has a higher ablation threshold, and a lower attenuation, resulting in the laser energy being deposited in a larger volume. Nevertheless, some superficial ablations were also observed at and . Regarding our results, the recommended clinical approach to support optimal ablation is to start with vascularized tissue or apply a thin layer of blood to the perimatrix of the cholesteatoma. The diode laser enables precise ablation in single-pulse mode by selecting the optimal power levels, distances and irradiation angles. It is a promising instrument for the controlled ablation of cholesteatoma tissue while protecting sensitive middle ear structures.

Single diode laser pulses enable precise ablation of cholesteatoma tissue while protecting the ossicular structures. The procedure therefore offers great potential for clinical use as a hearing-preserving supplement in cholesteatoma surgery.

sections.section: Preparation And Characterization Of Porcine Cartilage Models
sections.text: Cartilage samples from the external ear of pigs (slaughterhouse material) were used for the experimental investigations. The tissue was obtained commercially by the Medical Laser Center Lübeck from a slaughterhouse licensed according to European Union regulations (EC No. 853/2004 and EU 2017/625). The samples were transported to the laboratory in a cooled container and stored in a refrigerator at until further processing for a maximum of 3 h, with all experiments performed on the same day to ensure comparable tissue conditions. After cleaning the auricle thoroughly under running water, the remaining auricle was cut into strips approximately wide, avoiding all cartilage ridges. The superficial skin and fat layers were then removed manually with a scalpel (Swann-Morton, UK) and dissecting scissors (Hammacher, Germany). A thin layer of residual soft tissue remained on the cartilage surface. This served as a reference tissue model for the cholesteatoma that can form over the cartilage. The exposed cartilage tissue was removed with tweezers (Fuhrmann, Germany) and cut into square samples with an edge length of approximately . The finished samples were transferred to sterile 6-well plates (Greiner Bio-One, Austria) and stored there in Ringer’s solution until the experiment was carried out. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) was used to determine the thickness of the remaining soft tissue layer on top of the cartilage (Telesto with the OCT-LSM03-BB lens (Thorlabs, USA)). The thickness of the remaining tissue was between (Fig. 7 ). To increase absorption, a thin layer of porcine blood was applied on the sample surface before ablation (Fig. 7 ). This porcine blood was diluted with sodium citrate in a ratio of immediately after collection and frozen at . The blood underwent a controlled thawing process at throughout an entire night to achieve consistent conditions.

Human tissue samples were taken during clinical operations at the Department of Otolaryngology at the University Medical Center Schleswig–Holstein, Lübeck Campus. The samples were used after approval by the ethics committee (ethics vote: file number 2022–560). We confirm that all methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations (Declaration of Helsinki). Immediately after collection, the tissue samples were stored in physiological saline solution and processed within two hours for ablation experiments.

Tissue ablation was performed using a diode laser (Fox IV, A.R.C.) with a core diameter optical fiber (HighFlex, A.R.C., numerical aperture 0.22). This laser can be operated in a mode in which individual pulses (in our tests: ) can be triggered via the foot switch. Before each ablation was performed, it was necessary to apply a small amount of pig blood to the samples. This also helped to maintain a moist surface and reduce potential drying effects during the measurements. Tissue samples from both porcine cartilage and human tissue were used. The blood was applied using a thin brush, and the surface of the sample was dried with blotting paper before application to ensure the smallest possible and optimal blood layer height 25 . This enabled reproducible carbonization and simulated realistic surgical scenarios, which in turn allowed the volume removal and ablation depth to be measured. An image was then captured using a camera attachment (EOS 550D, Canon, Japan) on a microscope (Stemi SV8, Zeiss, Germany). The sample was then positioned on an adjustable sample table located below the fiber. The fiber was attached to a robotic arm (Rotrics DexArm, Rotrics, USA). The LM-10 thermopile sensor from Coherent USA measured power at the fiber end before each ablation test to confirm that test conditions remained constant. In the following experiments, the fiber was aligned over this initiation point. In order to take into account different scenarios during an operation, the distances between the tissue sample and the fiber, as well as the angles of the fiber to the sample, were systematically varied. Measurements were taken at distances of , , , and from the sample, with the angle of the fiber to the tissue sample always being (Fig. 8 ). Furthermore, the fiber was positioned at angles of , , , and to the sample, while the distance between the fiber and the sample was set to for this series of measurements (Fig. 8 ). The pulse length of the single pulse was always and was tested with different laser powers ( , , , and , corresponding to the power emitted during the laser pulse). Single pulses were used for the first experimental series, analogous to its use in surgical cholesteatoma resection. To simulate continuous tissue ablation, in another experiment series of 10 individual spots were applied on porcine cartilage samples (with a small amount of blood on top, as described above). The distance between the spot centers was or (Fig. 8 ). In half of the samples, a tissue layer thickness of approximately was left. A distinction is made between “less tissue thickness” ( ) and “higher tissue thickness” ( ). The applied laser power was with a pulse duration of . The fiber spacing was kept constant at . sections.section: Evaluation Of Ablation Craters And Tissue Damage
sections.text: Optical coherence tomography (OCT, see section " Preparation and characterization of porcine cartilage models ") was used to measure the depth and width of the laser ablation craters. The lateral resolution is , the axial resolution . Cross-sectional B-scans were analyzed to determine the distance between the crater edges and the deepest point. Each measurement was repeated three times to minimize error. After OCT evaluation, the tissue samples were embedded in Tissue-Tek Cryomold molds ( ) using Tissue Freezing Medium (Leica), frozen at , and then cut into thick sections using a 2800 Frigocut cryostat (Reichert-Jung). Sections were taken at different positions along the laser spot and stained with hematoxylin–eosin (H&E) according to a modified Carl Roth Rapid Staining Kit protocol. Stained sections were examined under an inverted microscope (Nikon) at and magnification. Both overall images and detailed views of the ablated areas were analyzed, and the open-source software Fiji was used for quantitative evaluation of the damaged areas.
